passage: I'm Bhupen, and I saw my sister Sabina roll her eyes when Ma asked her to fold the clothes. Ma's face went tight. “What was that?” “Nothing.” I couldn't tell if Sabina was bored, tired from school, or still angry about the argument earlier. Ma took a breath. “Sabina, you seem fed up. What's up?” Sabina sat down on the bed. “I've folded the clothes three times this week and Bhupen never does.” Ma nodded. “Fair. Bhupen, you do it tomorrow.” I sulked, but it was fair.

qa.q: What did Ma ask Sabina to fold?
qa.a: She asked her to fold the clothes.

qa.q: What was Sabina probably feeling behind the eye-roll, and what else could it have been?
qa.a: Fed up, because she felt the chore was unfair, as she said she had folded the clothes three times and Bhupen never does. It could also have been tiredness or boredom, as Bhupen guessed.

qa.q: How did Ma's question open a better talk?
qa.a: She named that Sabina seemed fed up and asked what was up, instead of arguing about the eye-roll. That let the real complaint come out.

qa.q: How does Bhupen feel about the outcome?
qa.a: He sulked, but he admits it was fair, so he seems to feel a bit caught out and also accepts it. 😅

grounding: An eye-roll signals annoyance and a calm question opens a better talk.

passage:
Monday: when Ms Anjali reminded the class about the spelling test, Elizabeth rolled her eyes. Ms Anjali said nothing but noticed.
Wednesday: Elizabeth rolled her eyes again. After class Ms Anjali said calmly, “I noticed the eye-roll. What's going on?” Elizabeth shrugged. “The words are too easy. I finish first and wait.” Ms Anjali nodded. “Thank you for telling me.”
Friday: Ms Anjali handed Elizabeth an extra list of long words. There was no eye-roll. Elizabeth said, “Can I have the hardest one first?”

qa.q: On which day did Ms Anjali ask Elizabeth what was going on?
What was Elizabeth probably feeling when she rolled her eyes on Monday, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Probably bored, since she later said the words were too easy and she finishes first and waits. It could also have been mild annoyance at being reminded.

qa.q: How did Ms Anjali's approach work better than scolding?
qa.a: She calmly asked what was going on, so Elizabeth explained, and the answer led to an extra list that solved the boredom.

qa.q: How might Ms Anjali have felt when she first saw the eye-roll?
qa.a: Possibly a little stung or puzzled, but she said nothing and waited to ask privately. That gave her a real answer instead of an argument.

grounding: An eye-roll signals boredom or annoyance; calmly asking what is wrong opens a better conversation.
